chief_complaint: rapidly spreading, exquisitely tender, warm, fiery red plaque with raised sharply demarcated borders across right cheek and ear (Erysipelas)
hpi_details: 68F presents with 24-hour rapid onset of a bright red, swollen, hot, and painful rash spreading across her right cheek, nose, and over her right earlobe. Experienced high shaking chills and headache 6 hours before the rash appeared. Rash is extremely tender and feels raised and firm to touch. Patient has mild baseline swelling in her right leg and diabetes.
ideas: thinks she caught a severe facial skin infection or shingles
concerns: feeling extremely lethargic, feverish, and scared by how fast the redness is moving across her face
expectations: wants immediate IV antibiotics and pain relief
pmh: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Lymphedema of right leg

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Facial Erysipelas is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes admitting to general medicine/dermatology given facial localization, high fever, and diabetes, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: rapidly spreading, exquisitely tender, warm, fiery red plaque with raised sharply demarcated borders across right cheek and ear (Erysipelas)

Key HPI features: 68F presents with 24-hour rapid onset of a bright red, swollen, hot, and painful rash spreading across her right cheek, nose, and over her right earlobe. Experienced high shaking chills and headache 6 hours before the rash appeared. Rash is extremely tender and feels raised and firm to touch. Patient has mild baseline swelling in her right leg and diabetes.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 115, BP 122/76, Temp 39.3C. Facial exam demonstrates a brilliant fiery-red, tense, indurated, warm plaque involving the right malar cheek, bridging across the nasal bridge to the left inner cheek, and extending onto the right earlobe (Milian's ear sign positive: because the earlobe lacks subcutaneous fat, involvement confirms superficial dermal/lymphatic localization distinguishing erysipelas from deep cellulitis). The border between infected and normal skin is sharply demarcated, raised, and step-like. Right submandibular lymphadenopathy present.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Lymphedema of right leg
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Facial Erysipelas.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis (less sharply demarcated) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever with rapid spread across the face — risk of orbital or intracranial spread.
management_principles: Admit to general medicine/dermatology given facial localization, high fever, and diabetes

Initiate parenteral IV antibiotics targeting streptococci: IV Penicillin G (2-4 million units q4h) or IV Cefazolin (1g q8h) until fever and erythema resolve, then transition to oral Penicillin V or Cephalexin to complete a 10-14 day course
Provide cool saline compresses and elevate head of bed
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: rapidly spreading, exquisitely tender, warm, fiery red plaque with raised sharply demarcated borders across right cheek and ear (Erysipelas)

68F presents with 24-hour rapid onset of a bright red, swollen, hot, and painful rash spreading across her right cheek, nose, and over her right earlobe. Experienced high shaking chills and headache 6 hours before the rash appeared. Rash is extremely tender and feels raised and firm to touch. Patient has mild baseline swelling in her right leg and diabetes.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 115, BP 122/76, Temp 39.3C. Facial exam demonstrates a brilliant fiery-red, tense, indurated, warm plaque involving the right malar cheek, bridging across the nasal bridge to the left inner cheek, and extending onto the right earlobe (Milian's ear sign positive: because the earlobe lacks subcutaneous fat, involvement confirms superficial dermal/lymphatic localization distinguishing erysipelas from deep cellulitis). The border between infected and normal skin is sharply demarcated, raised, and step-like. Right submandibular lymphadenopathy present.
reference_soap.assessment: Facial Erysipelas (St. Anthony's Fire) with systemic inflammatory response, secondary to Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).
reference_soap.plan: Admit to general medicine/dermatology given facial localization, high fever, and diabetes. Initiate parenteral IV antibiotics targeting streptococci: IV Penicillin G (2-4 million units q4h) or IV Cefazolin (1g q8h) until fever and erythema resolve, then transition to oral Penicillin V or Cephalexin to complete a 10-14 day course. Provide cool saline compresses and elevate head of bed.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Erysipelas (superficial dermal/lymphatic infection, sharply demarcated raised borders, bright fiery redness, sudden onset with rigors, caused overwhelmingly by Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus) from Cellulitis (deep subcutaneous tissue infection, ill-defined indistinct borders, pinkish erythema, slower onset, caused by both Strep and Staph aureus)
Evaluate Milian's ear sign (involvement of earlobe confirming erysipelas over cellulitis due to anatomical lack of subcutaneous fat in the pinna)

Select targeted narrow-spectrum beta-lactam therapy (Penicillin G, Amoxicillin, or Cefazolin) for streptococcal erysipelas without unnecessarily over-covering for MRSA unless purulence or trauma is present

Identify predisposing risk factors for recurrent lower extremity erysipelas/cellulitis (lymphedema, tinea pedis interdigital fissures, chronic venous insufficiency) and implement prophylaxis protocols

teaching.one_liner: A superficial bacterial skin infection, typically Group A Streptococcus, causing a rapidly spreading, sharply demarcated, fiery-red, tender plaque on the face — treated with IV antibiotics given the location and systemic symptoms.
red_flags: High fever with rapid spread across the face — risk of orbital or intracranial spread

must_ask.say: How quickly did this redness spread across your face — over hours?
Does the redness have a sharp, raised edge?
Did you have chills or a headache before the rash appeared?
Is the area very painful and hot to touch?
Do you have diabetes or any leg swelling problems?
